<div class="learn-box">
**What you will learn**

Separate date sources from presentation, choose factor/number/date periods, extract parts, calculate anchored ages, and handle partial dates explicitly.
</div>

**You need:** the client packages and the Opal login from
[Getting started](book-00-start.html). This chapter uses `omop.questionnaire`,
the synthetic questionnaire study described there.

## Start this chapter

Log in first:




``` r
library(dsOMOPClient)
conns <- ds.omop.login("https://localhost:8443", user = "administrator",
  password = "password", resource = "omop.questionnaire", server = "site")$conns
```



The connection is ready; `conns` identifies the server used by the analysis calls.

## A date source and a presentation are separate

A *source* says which date to use. A *date specification* says how to represent it.
`first_visit`, `death`, `birth`, `index`, `index_end`, observation bounds, a fixed
ISO date and `omop_anchor(event)` are date sources. An ISO date is written
`YYYY-MM-DD`, independently of the analyst's locale.


``` r
first_visit <- omop_date("first_visit")
```

With no specification this is an exact R Date assigned privately on the server.
It does not download a date vector. We can inspect the column inventory:


``` r
exact <- omop_recipe(variables = list(visit_date = first_visit),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
recipe_execute(exact, out = c(people = "D_date_exact"), datasources = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_date_exact", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> $site
#> [1] "person_id"  "visit_date"
```

The schema contains the protected person key and `visit_date`. The 12 people
without visits keep a missing date. Native `omop_date()` and ordinary
`first_date`/`last_date` reducers differ: those reducers without a date specification
return day offsets. The [visit walkthrough](book-13-visits.html) compares both.

## Month periods as categories

A *period* is a calendar block, such as a month or quarter. Its default presentation
is an ordered factor: categories with a defined chronological order.


``` r
month_spec <- omop_date_spec(precision = "month", representation = "factor",
  level_range = c("2020-03-01", "2020-07-31"))
```

The public range declares common levels, including empty months. It never filters
observed dates. Do not derive a “public” range from private minimum/maximum dates.


``` r
months <- omop_recipe(variables = list(month = omop_date("first_visit", month_spec)),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
recipe_execute(months, out = c(people = "D_date_months"), datasources = conns)
```

``` r
ds.omop.table("D_date_months", "month", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> Combined (all valid sites): month 
#> D_date_months$month
#> 2020-03 2020-04 2020-05 2020-06 2020-07 
#>      12       0       0      12      12 
#> 
#> By site:
#>                    study
#> D_date_months$month site
#>             2020-03   12
#>             2020-04    0
#>             2020-05    0
#>             2020-06   12
#>             2020-07   12
```

March, June and July each contain 12 first visits; another 12 people have
no visit and are omitted from this table. `ds.omop.table()` excludes missing
values while retaining declared zero categories such as April and May. Ordered factors have ordered-factor
model contrasts; for a linear time trend request a number explicitly.

## Periods as numbers


``` r
numbers <- omop_recipe(variables = list(month_index = omop_date("first_visit",
  omop_date_spec(precision = "month", representation = "number",
    numeric = "index", origin = "2020-01-01"))),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
recipe_execute(numbers, out = c(people = "D_date_numbers"), datasources = conns)
```

``` r
dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_date_numbers$month_index", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "integer"
#> 
#> $site$length
#> [1] 48
#> 
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>       5%      10%      25%      50%      75%      90%      95%     Mean 
#> 2.000000 2.000000 2.000000 5.000000 6.000000 6.000000 6.000000 4.333333
```

``` r
dsBaseClient::ds.numNA("D_date_numbers$month_index", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> $site
#> [1] 12
```

January 2020 is zero, February one and March two. The mean 4.33 averages
indices 2, 5 and 6 across 36 visitors; 12 are missing. These numbers identify
calendar months, not time since a birthday. Year/fiscal-year numbers instead
use the year; `numeric = "decimal_year"` supplies a fractional year.

## Periods as boundary dates


``` r
month_start <- omop_date("first_visit",
  omop_date_spec(precision = "month", representation = "start"))
month_end <- omop_date("first_visit",
  omop_date_spec(precision = "month", representation = "end"))
```

Start and end are Date objects, with inclusive month bounds. They deliberately
coarsen the original day; they do not claim that the visit occurred at a boundary.


``` r
bounds <- omop_recipe(variables = list(start = month_start, end = month_end),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
recipe_execute(bounds, out = c(people = "D_date_bounds"), datasources = conns)
ds.omop.mutate("D_date_bounds", days = end - start + 1L,
  newobj = "D_month_lengths", datasources = conns)
```

``` r
dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_month_lengths$days", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "integer"
#> 
#> $site$length
#> [1] 48
#> 
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>       5%      10%      25%      50%      75%      90%      95%     Mean 
#> 30.00000 30.00000 30.00000 31.00000 31.00000 31.00000 31.00000 30.66667
```

``` r
dsBaseClient::ds.numNA("D_month_lengths$days", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> $site
#> [1] 12
```

The mean inclusive month length is 30.67 days across 36 visitors: March and
July have 31 days, June has 30. The 12 people with no visit remain missing.
The inclusive length adds one day. Different months need different lengths;
a fixed 30-day bin is a different definition.

## Extract date parts

A *part* is a component such as year, month or weekday. Named entries choose the
final column names in this bundle.


``` r
parts <- omop_recipe(variables = list(visit = omop_date_parts("first_visit",
  c(visit_year = "year", visit_month = "month", weekday = "weekday_name"))),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
recipe_execute(parts, out = c(people = "D_date_parts"), datasources = conns)
```

``` r
ds.omop.table("D_date_parts", "weekday", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> Combined (all valid sites): weekday 
#> D_date_parts$weekday
#>    Monday   Tuesday Wednesday  Thursday    Friday  Saturday    Sunday 
#>        24         0         0         0         0        12         0 
#> 
#> By site:
#>                     study
#> D_date_parts$weekday site
#>            Monday      24
#>            Tuesday      0
#>            Wednesday    0
#>            Thursday     0
#>            Friday       0
#>            Saturday    12
#>            Sunday       0
```

The first visits fall on Saturday for 12 people and Monday for 24; another 12
people have no visit and are omitted here. Weekday names use fixed English levels, with Monday first. Month categories
likewise include all twelve months. Year, ISO week/year, quarter, day-of-year and
cyclic sine/cosine parts are also available. For season parts, declare the intended hemisphere (the default is north);
using only a week number without its week-year can mix different years.

<div class="book-tip">
**Tip**

Choose a calendar number for a time trend and an elapsed duration for time between events. They answer different questions.
</div>

## Ages at any anchor

`omop_age_at()` measures completed birthdays at the chosen date. The anchor below
selects the first education observation for each person, not the first visit.
Education question is **900001**, found in [chapter 4](book-04-vocabulary.html).


``` r
education_date <- omop_anchor(omop_event("observation", concepts = 900001L))
ages <- omop_recipe(variables = list(at_death = omop_age_at("death"),
  at_question = omop_age_at(education_date)),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
recipe_execute(ages, out = c(people = "D_date_ages"), datasources = conns)
```

``` r
dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_date_ages$at_death",
  useNA = "always", datasources = conns)$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
```

```
#> D_date_ages$at_death
#> 32 33 42 43 NA 
#>  6  6  6  6 24
```

Six people each died at completed ages 32, 33, 42 and 43. The 24 missing ages
come from 12 people with no death and 12 with an incomplete birth date.
A table makes these few ages clearer than interpolated summary quantiles. A February 29 birthday
completes on March 1 in a non-leap year. Exact age does not equal year subtraction.


``` r
dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_date_ages$at_question",
  useNA = "always", datasources = conns)$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
```

```
#> D_date_ages$at_question
#> 29 39 NA 
#> 12 12 24
```

At the first education question, 12 people were 29 and 12 were 39; the
24 without that question have no age at that anchor. The event sets a different
age reference. An index, an observation bound
or a fixed ISO date works through the same API.

## Partial dates: retain what is known

Twelve people have a birth year but no birth month or day. The default `partial =
"none"` keeps an invariant year but cannot invent a day or completed age.


``` r
partial <- omop_recipe(variables = list(birth_year = omop_date("birth",
  omop_date_spec(precision = "year"))),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
recipe_execute(partial, out = c(people = "D_date_partial"), datasources = conns)
```

``` r
ds.omop.table("D_date_partial", "birth_year", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> Combined (all valid sites): birth_year 
#> D_date_partial$birth_year
#> 1975 1980 1990 2000 
#>   12   12   12   12 
#> 
#> By site:
#>                          study
#> D_date_partial$birth_year site
#>                      1975   12
#>                      1980   12
#>                      1990   12
#>                      2000   12
```

Each birth-year category contains 12 people: 1975, 1980, 1990 and 2000.
All 48 birth years are known even though 12 exact birthdays are not. If the study permits an estimate, declare
imputation instead of letting an implicit convention choose it.


``` r
estimated <- omop_recipe(variables = list(age = omop_age_at("death",
  date_spec = omop_date_spec(partial = "mid"))),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
recipe_execute(estimated, out = c(people = "D_date_estimated"), datasources = conns)
```

``` r
dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_date_estimated$age",
  useNA = "always", datasources = conns)$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
```

```
#> D_date_estimated$age
#> 23 24 32 33 42 43 NA 
#>  6  6  6  6  6  6 12
```

The estimate adds six people aged 23 and six aged 24. Missing age at death
falls from 24 to 12; the remaining 12 have no death date. The middle possible
birth day supplies an **estimated** completed age. `start` and
`end` use the first/last possible day. `unit = "annual_years"` explicitly asks
for calendar-year subtraction instead. Invalid components stay missing even
with imputation. `future = "na"` requires a fixed `as_of` date; do not use a moving
“today” cutoff in a reproducible plan.

## Custom labels without arbitrary date code


``` r
custom <- omop_recipe(variables = list(month = omop_date("first_visit",
  omop_date_spec(precision = "custom", pattern = "%b %Y"))),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
recipe_execute(custom, out = c(people = "D_date_custom"), datasources = conns)
```

``` r
ds.omop.table("D_date_custom", "month", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> Combined (all valid sites): month 
#> D_date_custom$month
#> Mar_2020 Jun_2020 Jul_2020 
#>       12       12       12 
#> 
#> By site:
#>                    study
#> D_date_custom$month site
#>            Mar_2020   12
#>            Jun_2020   12
#>            Jul_2020   12
```

The counts are again 12 each for Mar 2020, Jun 2020 and Jul 2020; the 12
missing visits are omitted. Only the month labels have changed. This uses fixed English month
abbreviations and a year. The supported directives
are `%Y`, `%m`, `%d`, `%j`, `%G`, `%V`, `%u`, `%b`, `%B`, `%a`, `%A` and `%%`,
with simple literal text/punctuation. ISO weeks require `%G-W%V`, not `%Y-W%V`.
Arbitrary `strftime` directives, locale-dependent code and time-of-day are refused.
A named `labels` map may rename public date categories but must keep them unique;
it cannot merge dates. Fine-grained factor labels still face disclosure checks.

## Other calendar systems

| Precision | Meaning or required declaration |
|---|---|
| year, semester, quarter, month | Calendar year; halves, quarters, months |
| iso_week | Monday weeks; week 1 has at least four new-year days |
| cdc_week | Sunday weeks; week 1 has at least four new-year days |
| epi_week | Supply `week_start` and `week_min_days` |
| fiscal_year, fiscal_semester, fiscal_quarter, fiscal_month | Choose `fiscal_start` (default January); labels name the starting year |
| relative_days | Supply an anchor for day offsets |
| day | Exact private Date |
| custom | Restricted public pattern |

For example, choose an April-start fiscal quarter explicitly:


``` r
fiscal <- omop_recipe(variables = list(quarter = omop_date("first_visit",
  omop_date_spec(precision = "fiscal_quarter", fiscal_start = 4L))),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
recipe_execute(fiscal, out = c(people = "D_date_fiscal"), datasources = conns)
```

``` r
ds.omop.table("D_date_fiscal", "quarter", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> Combined (all valid sites): quarter 
#> D_date_fiscal$quarter
#> 2019-FQ4 2020-FQ1 2020-FQ2 
#>       12       12       12 
#> 
#> By site:
#>                      study
#> D_date_fiscal$quarter site
#>              2019-FQ4   12
#>              2020-FQ1   12
#>              2020-FQ2   12
```

March maps to 2019-FQ4, June to 2020-FQ1 and July to 2020-FQ2, with 12
people each. The 12 missing visits are omitted. March belongs to the preceding fiscal year. The variable's specification overrides
the recipe's specification, which overrides the defaults.

## Try it

Calculate elapsed days from first visit to death and request a summary. Why are some values missing?

<details><summary>Solution</summary>


``` r
elapsed <- omop_recipe(variables = list(days = omop_time_between("first_visit", "death")),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
recipe_execute(elapsed, out = c(people = "D_date_elapsed"), datasources = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.summary("D_date_elapsed$days", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> $site
#> $site$class
#> [1] "integer"
#> 
#> $site$length
#> [1] 48
#> 
#> $site$`quantiles & mean`
#>       5%      10%      25%      50%      75%      90%      95%     Mean 
#> 1095.000 1095.000 1095.000 1362.500 1461.000 1630.000 1630.000 1334.333
```

``` r
dsBaseClient::ds.numNA("D_date_elapsed$days", datasources = conns)
```

```
#> $site
#> [1] 12
```
The mean duration is 1,334.33 days, with 36 valid durations and 12 missing, because 12 people have neither
a visit nor a death date. Elapsed days need both dates. This calculation does not need a complete birth date, unlike exact age. It is a duration, not a calendar label.

</details>

## Exercise 2: distinguish a period from a duration

Which variable represents a calendar category and which measures elapsed time?
Confirm using the short descriptions from `recipe_explain()`.

<details><summary>Solution 2</summary>


``` r
month_explanation <- recipe_explain(months)$text
duration_explanation <- recipe_explain(elapsed)$text
writeLines(grep("^  (month|days):", c(month_explanation, duration_explanation), value = TRUE))
```

```
#>   month: calendar_date
#>   days: time_between
```

`calendar_date` identifies the calendar variable; its definition above chooses
month precision. `time_between` identifies the elapsed-days variable, whose
definition measures first visit to death. A calendar
period and a day duration answer different questions.

</details>

## Exercise 3: a pitfall to avoid

Export the month recipe. Does the JSON contain dates from the definition,
patient dates, or both?

<details><summary>Solution 3</summary>


``` r
json <- recipe_export_json(months)
writeLines(grep("2020-03-01|2020-07-31", strsplit(json, "\n")[[1]], value = TRUE))
```

```
#>         "level_range": ["2020-03-01", "2020-07-31"]
```

The public `level_range` dates 2020-03-01 and 2020-07-31 appear because we
declared them. JSON contains study definitions, including any fixed `origin`
or `as_of` dates, but no extracted patient dates. This is why “no dates in JSON”
would be the wrong claim.

</details>
## Recap

Choose a source, precision and representation. Partial information stays partial unless you declare estimation. Exact dates and ages remain private server columns.

**Next:** [10. Concepts as categories](book-10-harmonise.html).
